title: Part 6
text: throat, heavy and biological and wrong. Water surged backward down the hall, nearly dragging Orela into a wall. The next moment it shifted again, dragging Jake sideways into a doorframe. Lockers drifted like battering rams. Ceiling panels dropped seemingly at random. A pipe blew just above Leon’s head, vapor hissing out before water collapsed down like a fist. He ducked, snarling, shaking it off. The school wasn't trying to just drown them anymore. It was trying to tire them out first. The alcove appeared near the end of the hallway, as Danny had predicted. Orela's beam caught the edge of it mid-stroke — a break in the wall, barely three feet across, tucked into the corridor like the building had forgotten to fill it in. One side was boarded up, the planks swollen and dark, water seeping through the gaps in thin steady threads that ran the wrong direction. Not draining out. Coming in, as if the entire building had gone under and the pressure outside was simply looking for the path of least resistance. Every surge that rolled down the hallway made the planks flex, a subtle outward bow that suggested they had opinions about the situation and were getting louder about them. The roar was marginally less here, enough that they didn’t need to scream to be heard. Orela pushed Danny and Dwight back into the nearby wall, using her body to brace them. She swept the flashlight across the warped planks, reading them, then felt Leon's hand close around hers and take the light. He moved to the boards, running his palm across the grain, pressing at the edges, testing the flex. His jaw worked once as he bit down the urge to try and slam into it himself. Everyone had tried unsuccessfully to break one of these at some point in their time in the Fog, almost always hurting themselves in the process. The killers always made it look so easy. Leon swept the flashlight across the planks one more time, jaw set, and stepped back. He looked at Danny, gesturing to the blockage. “Think you can break it?” Danny looked at the planks. Looked at his own hands, still faintly trembling from the hallway. The robes were gone. The mask was gone. The terror radius, the cloak, all of it — gone. He'd been running on borrowed time since the moment the school flinched, and he knew what that meant better than any of them. The Entity's gifts came as a package. You didn't get to keep the strength while She took back everything else. Or at least, he was fairly sure you didn't. He had no way to know for certain because killers didn't lose their gifts. Killers didn't end up treading water in a flooding preschool wondering if they still worked. “I’m really not sure anymore.” Leon helped pull him into the alcove, bracing against the current as best he could so Danny didn’t get torn away on him. “Well, you’re the only one of us with the clearance card. And it’s not like we have other options here.” The alcove gave them maybe two feet of working space behind Danny, which wasn't much, but it was something. He braced his back against the opposite wall, assessed the planks, and tried not to think too hard about the specific question sitting in the middle of his chest. Technically they weren’t wrong. He'd broken killer walls before. Hundreds of times, probably — the muscle memory of it was there, the particular angle and force and follow-through. That part wasn't the problem. The problem was that everything else had already been taken back. If he didn’t have the Entity’s strength, he doubted his normal human strength would be enough to crack it, let alone break it. She hadn’t shown any signs that She intended to spare him, so why would She give him such an easy out? But what choice did he have? He couldn’t just wallow in his sudden abandonment when he was just as screwed as the survivors. He needed to be useful, which was a different thing entirely and required not having someone treating him like he was about to fall over. He could fall over later. Right now, he squared his hips to the wall, pulled his knee up, and drove his heel into the planks. The kick landed solid through the water drag, the impact rattling back up through his hip and spine, water spraying across him in a sharp burst that made him flinch. His shoulders cracked against the wall behind him, jostling his ribs and reminding him of just how many were likely cracked. The planks made an awful sound under the impact, but he could feel it through his leg. It hadn’t shifted. Danny gritted his teeth. He hadn’t felt abandoned before. Not really. Not until now. If he couldn’t get this wall open, what then? He could barely manage to stand in this current unaided. What if they realized he wasn’t worth the extra hands to keep afloat? Leon shifted his grip on Danny’s arm and he jerked it away, moving to try again. He didn't have the breath to explain it and didn't particularly want to — the reasoning was simple enough, if not flattering. He'd already been hauled out of a hallway once tonight. He'd already been stripped of his gear while he stood there and let it happen. He was not going to stand in an alcove and be held upright like something that needed managing while he tried to do the one useful thing left available to him. This couldn’t afford to fail. They were going to leave him to Her fury; he just knew it. He slammed his heel against the wood, harder. The impact sent a dull crack of pain across his hip and up through his spine, water spraying into his face from the force of it. His shoulders took the wall behind him. The planks bent — actually bent, a visible bow outward, the wood flexing against the pressure — and the sound they made was significantly worse than the first time. They held. Danny stared at the bend in the wood. The water lapped at him. The thought floated up unwanted like debris in his mind— they had no reason to keep protecting him if he wasn't of use here. With how often he had hunted them, they would let the current take him back into the dark, and he would deserve it. Distracted by that thought, the third kick missed its mark — his foot sliding wildly off the slick surface and sending him under with a surprised squawk — and the current had him immediately, pulling him sideways through a forest of legs in the dark. A hand caught his wrist, halting his momentum and jolting his shoulder hard enough to hurt, dragging him up and back into the air. He broke the surface sputtering, shaking water from his eyes, and found Dwight — one hand locked around his wrist, the other braced against the alcove wall, breathing hard. Shaking visibly. The ghost of something that wasn't quite a smile on his face, there and gone, the universal language of now we're even. So, they didn’t just let him go after all. Well. Alright then. Leon straightened, shoving his hair back from his face, water streaming off his shoulders. He stared at the planks. Ran the logic again. The wall had flexed. It had made the sound. It should have worked — by any reasonable measure of force applied to material, it should have given at least a little more than it did. “Why didn’t it work? It should have worked. You guys break these all the time!” Danny looked back at him, ribs aching, hip singing from the second impact. “I think... I think She might have fired me. The strength, the cloak... I don't know how long ago. I don't know if I have any of it left." David's expression went through several things in quick succession as he let out a low, venomous snort. That was it. That was the final goddamn straw. “Well, that’s just fucking great.” He pulled Leon aside, fitting himself in the alcove. “Killer wall, no killer strength. Fantastic.” He glared at the boards like they were a personal insult; his shoulder still raw from the back door, lungs burning, chest rattling. “We don’t have TIME for this shit!” He planted his back against the opposite wall, and tilted his chin up from the waterline until he had an inch of air. Looked at the planks. Looked at the ceiling. Took the deepest breath he could manage. Then with a deliberate jump, he drove both legs into the wall with everything he had. The impact hit with a deep, booming crack, felt more than heard, the shock of it traveling up through the floor and into the legs of everyone in the alcove. The planks shuddered — the whole frame shuddered — and the seeping water coming through the gaps turned abruptly to jets, thin hard streams spraying into the dark. David dropped sharply into the dark, water closing over him for one ungraceful second before he found the floor and shoved himself back up, resetting position against the wall and squaring up for another go. “Wait, seriously?” Danny pulled himself higher on Orela’s shoulder, trying to keep his face up. “Do you have any idea how much force it takes to crack that thing??” “You got a better idea?!” He'd broken killer walls. Knew exactly what it took — the particular combination of mass and force and the Entity's gifts behind it, the whole apparatus working together. Without the gifts, the math didn't work. A normal person hitting a killer wall was just a person hitting a very solid wall, and the wall won, and that was the end of it. David hit it again. The sound that came back was wrong. Not the dead thud everything else had made that night — something that carried, that traveled through the water in a pressure wave Danny felt in his teeth. The planks screamed. The whole frame shuddered, the seeping water through the gaps surging to angry jets that sprayed into the dark in thin hard streams. David dropped with the recoil, no support behind him, and was back in position before the current could make a decision about it. The alcove tried to evict him anyway. The surge came from behind, the current finding the narrow space and accelerating through it, and David's footing went sideways. Jake lunged in to catch him, one hand locked around his arm, his uninjured leg wedged against a locker in the corridor like a human doorstop. He was coughing between breaths, the wet rattle of it sitting deep in his lungs, but his grip didn't waver. Leon angled the flashlight. David's face in the beam looked wild. There was no strategy in it, no calculation. All the light could see in his eyes was rage and stubborn determination. He found the wall again with both feet. The boards flexed. Held. But the sound they made on the way back — the long, low groan of wood pushed past what it had agreed to handle — for the first time it sounded like they might actually break. Ch 10 – Suspension The rest of the space between the waterline and the ceiling vanished smoothly. Four feet of it, then three, then two — the ceiling arriving in steady increments as the water found the last of the space and claimed it. They tipped their heads back, chins up, buying seconds. The pipes screamed above them, muffled now, translated by the water into something felt rather than heard. The lockers, the debris, the building's ongoing commentary — all of it reduced to pressure and distant collision, arriving through the water as vibration rather than sound. And then the surface closed. The noise the school had been making all night compressed into silence. David's kicks traveled through it in short concussive thuds, rhythmic and close, nearly as present as their own heartbeats. Everything else was stillness and dark and the heavy press of water from every direction. Leon let the flashlight go. He dropped it deliberately, the beam slowly eaten into the black as the current washed it down the hallway. He needed the extra hand to help anchor himself against the wall. Being able to see didn’t matter anymore. Either the wall broke and they wouldn’t need the light, or... He shook the thought off before it finished and turned his focus to the wall at his back and the person beside him. That was the whole job now. Stay still. Stay against the wall. Don't let the current make a decision for either of them. He got his arm around Dwight and pressed them both flat, narrowing the target, willing the water to find something else to pull at. Dwight's hand found his sleeve. The grip was immediate and tight, trembling in small, hiccupped pulses that Leon felt more than registered — every second stretching out longer than it should. He couldn’t reassure the man beyond tightening his own grip, so he just let the hand stay and kept them both against the wall and counted David's kicks moving through the water like a second heartbeat. Dwight held on. He couldn't tell if his eyes were open. The dark was the same either way, complete and total, pressing in from every direction. He didn't fight it. Years of trials had put something in him that wasn't courage exactly but functioned like it in emergencies — a flat, stubborn refusal to spend energy on what couldn't be helped. He was scared. He was tired. He was not particularly strong. But he could be still. He could last, if he stayed calm, if he kept his grip and kept his lungs and didn't think about how much time was passing. He could last. Probably. The movement hit them from the side without warning — a flurry of it, close, maybe two feet away in the dark, turbulent enough that the current shifted and tugged at his legs with new intent. His hand tightened on Leon's sleeve. He felt Leon go rigid beside him. Neither of them reached out. Moving meant opening up to the current. Moving meant losing the wall. Moving meant finding out what that was, and there were only so many things it could be, and none of the options were ones they could think about right now without their bodies making a decision they weren't ready for. They focused instead on the contact points. The texture of sleeves under fingers. The wall against shoulders. David's kicks moving through the water like a pulse. That was everything. That was all there was. They stayed, anchored, and tried not to think about what was happening two feet away from them in the dark. Orela had wrapped her arms around Danny’s chest the moment the ceiling closed in. Now, pressed with her back tight to the wall, face tucked low and leaving small bubbles in his hair, she was holding him there — keeping him still. Danny's hands were clamped over her arms, tight enough to hurt, as if her arms were all that stood between him and the darkness. She could feel the small hitches moving through him at irregular intervals, his body working against the stillness she needed from both of them. She'd registered the wheeze in his breathing before they went under. Had noted it and filed it and told herself it was manageable. Down here, she could feel it — the shallow quality of what he'd managed to grab before the water took the last of the air, the way each hitch cost him more than it should have. Between the injuries from earlier and the exhaustion he hadn’t had nearly as much time as the others to recover from, he hadn’t managed to get a proper breath before going under. She held him tighter and kept still and counted David's kicks moving through the water and tried not to let her hands shake. Her own lungs flared hot in her chest, but she focused only on him. If she could keep him still and calm, they both could make it. Danny knew exactly how much air he had left. That was the problem. In the hallway there hadn't been time to count — just the current and the dark and the animal insistence on the next breath. Down here there was nothing but time and stillness, and he had already gone in shorter than he would have preferred. He tried to be still. Tried to let Orela's grip be the thing doing the work, to stop spending what he had left on anything that wasn't strictly necessary. It almost worked. The need to move started low, barely there, and crept upward with patient incremental certainty until it wasn't a suggestion anymore. He shifted, a small involuntary thing, trying to suppress what was building in his chest, and felt Orela's arms tighten in response. Her palm pressed flat against his sternum. Taking inventory. He felt her go still in a different way — the careful conservation of before replaced by the specific stillness of someone who had suddenly understood something. His grip shifted on her arms without meaning to, fingers searching for leverage, and the thought that arrived alongside it was not a thought so much as a demand. Up. She felt it in his hands before he'd finished processing it. He fought it. That was the thing — he knew what was happening, could name it with the specific clarity that made it worse, and fought it anyway. The need had moved past suggestion and into instruction, his body delivering the message with increasing insistence regardless of what his brain had to say about it. He got his fingers under her arms and pulled, not hard, not yet, just testing the possibility of up. Her grip tightened. His chest was stuttering, stomach spasming beneath her elbow. Every instinct in him screamed to move, but she had him locked. One arm was iron across his sternum, the other pulling his abdomen as close as she could manage. Another hitch moved through him, sharper than the last, and his better judgment lost the argument. His hands found her wrists and pried, feet kicking for purchase, the animal logic of up, out, surface overriding everything else with a completeness that left no room for logic or reason. The current caught them from the side, almost dragging him out of her grip. She felt the twitch of a choice — that split second of fight or surrender — and chose for him. She didn’t stop to think. Just reached up and clapped her palm over his mouth and nose, fingers trembling with pressure, as she wrenched his head back against her shoulder to keep him from twisting away. She felt him register it. Felt the half second where he understood what she was doing and why. The next second, he exploded. His whole body torqued against her grip, one hard convulsive effort, hands clawing at her wrist, legs kicking at nothing. She held on. she wouldn’t lose him. Not like this. If he tore away now, they may never find him again. She needed to not lose him to the dark. She could deal with the fallout later. He bucked again, weaker, the reserves going fast, the water indifferent to how much he had left or how much he needed. She pressed his head back and held him flat and felt his chest seize against her palm, willing him to stop spending what he didn't have. Stop. Stop. Just stop. Please just pass out... His chest seized against her once, then again. She tightened her grip and held him there, a last blockade against the water, until the last jerk rolled through him like an aftershock — and stopped. She adjusted her grip and went still with him. Let her heart keep hammering against the fragile shape of his back. No wasted motion. Just a silent prayer that she hadn't just made the worst decision of the night. David felt every kick in his teeth. The concussive thud of each impact travelled up through the water and into his jaw, his chest, the base of his skull. Terror burned hotter than exhaustion now, driving his legs back into the planks over and over. The wall was talking back now in a way it hadn't been before, something in the structure of it shifting under the assault, the flex coming back different from the dead resistance of earlier. Jake had him. That was the other thing he could feel — the grip on his upper arm, firm and present, the anchor that kept the current from sweeping him out of the alcove every time the recoil took his footing. He didn't make any motion to acknowledge Jake there. Couldn't afford the shift in focus. The grip shifted. He felt it happen — the tight clamp of a hand around his arm loosening by degrees, reorganising, fingers finding the fabric of his sleeve instead. He didn't look. He hit the wall again and felt Jake adjust behind him with a small tremor and filed that away too, in the same place he'd filed the sparks at the edge of his vision that had been there for the last three kicks and weren't getting better. He shook off the sparks. He knew what they meant. He'd felt that particular warning before, in other contexts, and he filed it in the same place he'd filed Jake's shifting grip and the way his lungs had been sending strongly worded letters of protest. He re-braced. Drove his heels into the wall. The vibration that came back was different — not the solid protest of before but something finer. A true sound this time. Short, fragile, but cutting through everything with a single distant crack. He felt it in his feet. Felt the board flex inward and catch. There. His chest hitched once as he backed against the wall for another kick. David’s heart stuttered. He hauled himself back into position, boot slipping slightly— His anchor had vanished. Jake’s grip slid from his arm and dissolved into the black. David whipped his head around, shot a hand after him, and hit only water. He held the reach for one suspended beat — Jake — and then let his arm drop and put his back against the wall and found the angle again. No time. No point. Refocus. Either Jake had been swept. Or he— no. No. If the wall didn't come down, none of it mattered. None of them. The board had cracked. He'd heard it. He could feel the flex in it had changed, the resistance giving way to something that felt almost like progress, and there was nothing left in the world except that and the next kick and the one after that. Either the wall was breaking— Or they all were. Ch 11 – Emergence Outside, the school was quiet. The playground lay still in the perpetual night air, long shadows cast by nearby streetlamps highlighted half-rusted jungle gyms and faded spring riders in a sick yellow glow, the gentle chug of partially finished generators echoing through the otherwise silent domain. The only thing different than the usual calm was the water. It seeped through the cracks in the boarded wall in thin dark trails, following gravity down the planks and pooling in the mud below. The boards were dark with it, saturated, the wood swollen past its original shape. A low thump rolled through the wall from the inside. Heavy. Close. The planks creaked — a short, shrill sound, tight with strain — before a single long crack bloomed across the wood. For a moment, the stillness settled back in across the streets. The wall gave another small creak, the crack widened ever so slightly— —and everything gave way all at once. The boards detonated outward into the playground with a concussive force that scattered every crow on the fence in one explosive black cloud, as a building’s worth of black water tore free from the entranceway and coursed through the grass like a flash flood, churning up gravel and dirt. The school forcefully vomited itself into the playground. Planks cartwheeled across the yard. Plaster chunks hit the asphalt like cannon fire. A locker sailed overhead and buried itself in the fence with a shriek of metal on metal. Ceiling tiles skipped across the flooded grass like thrown stone. Debris churned through the bushes at the yard's edge, shredding leaves and snapping branches, the whole playground receiving everything the building had accumulated over the course of the night in a chaotic surge of flotsam. And among the wreckage, tumbling out in the tide of furniture and broken tile and the last of the flood — Six bodies. David ripped his head free of the water with a strangled gasp. The sound tore out of him raw and violent, barely a breath, more a seizure of the lungs finally allowed to do what they'd been screaming to do for the last sixty seconds. He dragged himself up onto his hands and knees above the receding flood, chest seizing, hacking until bile scorched the back of his throat. His vision pulsed with sparks — the same ones he'd been shaking off for the last four kicks, back with interest now, blotting the edges of everything in slow warning flares. Debris caught against his arms, adding to the small cuts and bruises as he fought to stay somewhat upright and out of the flood. His boots scrabbled uselessly against the flooded grass, the motion still live in his legs long after it had any purpose. His body hadn't gotten the message yet. The momentum still lived in him, still screamed move, survive, break through — the instruction running on without the emergency that had issued it, burning the last of whatever he'd found below exhaustion against ground that didn't need breaking. The tide began to recede just as David’s arms gave out, the school finally finding an end to the flood. He went forward into the churned grass and stayed there, breath hitching and hacking, fingers clawing at the mud like it could tether him to something solid. His whole body trembled, the ache in his limbs blooming hot and bitter, deep and cellular, acid poured straight into his veins. But he could hear them. Around him, near him, the sounds of other people equally wrecked and alive — retching, coughing, tumbling through the debris. He could hear them. He pressed his forehead into the mud and let out a breath that had been waiting a very long time. Thank god. Leon hit the grass rolling, momentum flinging him across the flooded yard in a sodden tumble of limbs. The instinct was faster than thought — knees finding ground, legs pushing, upright before he'd registered that he was out. His eyes were already sweeping the yard, already cataloguing shapes in the debris, already trying to find headcounts through full body coughs that slammed his brain against his skull. His system was filing protests from every direction and he was ignoring every single one of them on the grounds that there wasn't time. The ground tilted sharply under him, his legs buckling against the dizziness. He staggered as the flood tried removing his position, planting a foot wide to catch himself, jaw locked against the grey that was creeping in at the edges of his vision. Not yet. He just needed a second. Just needed to see that they were all— Jake hit him like a sack of wet concrete. Shot out of the flood sideways, completely boneless, no warning, no trajectory that gave Leon any time to brace, Jake's full weight colliding with his legs, making him turn to try and compensate, inevitably taking them both down. Leon went backwards, spine and shoulders catching a discarded locker with a crack that he felt in his back teeth, Jake slamming down alongside him in the receding water, half across his lap, neither of them moving for a moment. The world spun. Kept spinning. Leon's chest heaved, the flood pooling cold around his ankles as if it hadn't finished with him yet, his vision doing something deeply unhelpful at the edges. He tried to push himself upright. His arms had opinions about that. He tried again. His body made the decision for him — just a quiet, final withdrawal of cooperation, the accumulated debt of the last several hours coming due all at once. He felt it happening and couldn't stop it, could only register the specific indignity of going under sitting still, propped against a locker in a puddle, before it took him the rest of the way down. He slumped against the locker with a soft grunt, head tipping to one side as his systems flickered out. The collision knocked something loose in Jake's chest, and he coughed, rough and sputtering, like his body only just remembered how to exist. He hadn't known he needed it to. One moment he was in the dark of the alcove with David’s arm in his grip, and the next Leon's legs were there and the impact drove through him like a starting pistol, his body lurching into function on pure reflex. For a moment, nothing worked right. His chest hitched, trying to summon another round of hacking, the thin thread of air scraping through his throat like broken glass. Not enough. He convulsed once and managed to roll off Leon, collapsing sideways into the muddy grass as his insides revolted. Water. So much water. Too far in, too deep down.
